The short story: A game with a lot of depth. Both rewarding and frustrating. Often at the same time. Puzzles in the ads are only a very small part of the game. The long story: Like a few other people I've spoken with, I decided to try out this game based on the ads depicting it as a puzzle game. Evony is most decidedly not a puzzle game. Yes, there are puzzles you can solve, but you can only access a small number of them, plus a handful of weekly puzzles, on starting the game. To access more puzzles, you must upgrade the keep in your city. Before moving onto that, though, I would be amiss in pointing out that the in-game puzzles don't have the same panache as the ads depict. The puzzle animations in the ad depict much more visual effects than what you get in-game. Back to the city part. Evony is a strategy game at its heart. It's all about building your city. Gathering and producing resources. Growing your army. Fighting non-player character (NPC) monsters for treasure, and, of course, fighting other players. There's an amazing depth to the strategy portion, and it's my personal opinion that TGI should be hyping that feature in their ads, and not the puzzles. At the very basic, you work with four resource types for building, and four troop types for your army. But it doesn't stop there. Your city contains multiple buildings that control the level of each troop type, how many troops you can train at once. How many troops you can deploy from your city. You can fine tune how many of each resource production building you have in your city. Further, when you send troops out, whether it be for gathering or fighting, they are led by a general, and there are so many generals of various capability available to keep the game interesting. Generals can be upgraded and fine tuned as well, and equipped with items that you can craft to further tweak their abilities as well. Evony provides the player with many different ways to customize the way they play. Couple all this with the ability to join any number of alliances of other players, along with the very active weekly event schedules, makes Evony a very lively game to play. It's the depth and weekly activity, though, that also make the game quite frustrating to play. Unless you're willing to sink a chunk of change into the game, you'll need to be active on a daily basis. Even if you choose not to participate in the events, you run the risk of being attacked by other players at any time. To keep your city safe requires grinding for gems to purchase "truce agreements" (shields or "bubbles" as they're known in-game) to protect your city from attack. You are protected as a new player to the game, but only for a short amount of time. If you choose not to purchase any of the in-game packages, you will be presented with offers on a regular basis. They're not overly intrusive and can be dismissed pretty easily if you choose to go the "free to play" route. I can't blame the developers for this. They are, after all, in business to make money. I played Evony for three months before finally quitting. Despite having found a very supportive alliance, I had grown tired and frustrated of the constant grind just to keep my city safe from attack. It even got to the point where I was setting reminders on my phone to check the game. For those who are willing and able to be truly dedicated to it, it can be quite rewarding, but there's no easy way to safely take a break and come back a few days or a week later. The graphics in Evony are decent. Most of the play mechanics involve either scrolling around 3D isometric renderings of your city and the world map, or working with 2D screens to adjust sliders, buttons, etc. The artwork on the 2D screens is well done and animations are decent, if a bit repetitive. There can often be a lot of small text which can be difficult to read for someone with vision problems, like myself, so I recommend using a magnification feature or app.

THIS GAME IS FOR BULLIES. Despite the advertising, it is not a puzzle game. It is a city-builder/war game where you have to battle monsters and other players. On the surface, that's not an inherently bad thing. There are plenty of games like that which are fun and engaging to play. HOWEVER. The war aspect of this game is incredibly unbalanced. You have players with 300 Million Power running roughshod over players with 50,000 Power. More powerful players are just decimating the cities and troops of less powerful players, leaving those with less power completely unable to partake in any of the building/war aspects. You build up troops only to have them all die because someone with 100x more power than you decided you were an easy target. Joining an alliance doesn't offer any kind of help or protection, either, as all of the "power players" are in the same alliance and are invite-only. So you have to join a "less powered" alliance with other players who are just as vulnerable to attack/annihilation as you are. There's no way to avoid it. And there's no way to escape. This game randomly drops you into a random server when you start, and only allows you 3 days to switch servers. So by the time you realize your randomly-assigned server is trash being run by playground bullies, you have no way to switch servers. Your only option is to quit the game entirely. The devs would do well to either implement the ability to switch servers at any time, or to find some other way to balance the building/war aspects. I've tried to email and was left on read, so customer service doesn't much care about players, unless you're one of the "Super Powerful" bullies who makes the game so miserable for anyone else trying to play. It's a shame that they're catering to bullies in these ways, because there are nice people just trying to have fun and help each other out in alliances, but then one of the "Big Guys" comes through and suddenly every friend you've made is quitting the game because they've had enough of being bullied and futilely trying to build up their cities just to have all that work be obliterated due to some bully's malicious whim. False advertising. No fun. Poor customer service. I'd give it Zero Stars if I could.
